conversation_history.content: My psychiatrist wants me to try an antidepressant and I keep canceling the follow-up appointment. I've been doing it for three months.
Three months of canceling — something is really getting in the way. What's your hesitation about the medication?
I don't want to be dependent on something. I don't want to feel numbed out or like I'm not myself. I already have something that works for the anxiety.
What's been working for you?
I smoke every night. Without fail for about three years now. It completely takes the edge off, I can actually sleep, I stop ruminating. I don't know who I'd be without it at this point.
It sounds like it's become pretty central to how you function. What brings you in today if it's working that well?

critical_turn: My girlfriend. She says I've changed, that I'm not motivated anymore, that I cancel plans to stay home, that I'm not the person she met. And she's not entirely wrong. I haven't moved up at work in three years, I stopped going to the gym, I don't really make plans anymore. But weed is natural, it's legal where we live, doctors literally prescribe it for anxiety. The reason I keep refusing the antidepressant is I don't want to become dependent on something I can't function without. But honestly I cannot picture getting through a single day without smoking now. I just don't see it the way she does.

marker_annotations.contradiction: Client explicitly states his reason for refusing the antidepressant is not wanting 'to become dependent on something I can't function without,' and in the very same turn states he 'cannot picture getting through a single day without smoking now' — a direct, literal contradiction of the reasoning he has just used.
marker_annotations.ambivalence: Client acknowledges his girlfriend 'is not entirely wrong' and lists concrete areas of decline (career, physical health, social life), but closes with 'I just don't see it the way she does' — simultaneously validating and dismissing the same evidence, holding both positions without resolution.

hill_rationale: Per Hill (2020, Ch.11), the client exhibits a stark internal contradiction — the rationale used to avoid one substance is the exact description of his relationship with the current substance — and ambivalence in partially accepting evidence of harm while refusing its conclusion, both of which are readiness markers pointing toward productive motivational exploration.
